Interrogating
the Machine

Why the most effective attacks on large language models look less like exploits and more like interrogations, and what counter-intelligence tradecraft teaches the people defending them.

AI Red Teaming Counter-Intelligence 17 Nov 2026 19 min read
← Back to main

There is a classic elicitation training story. An intelligence officer sits down next to an off-duty sailor in a bar and remarks, casually and wrongly, that the other side's submarines are faster and have bigger propellers than his navy's. The sailor bristles and corrects him. Then he corrects the next mistake, and the one after that. Nobody asked him a question. He volunteered the details himself, to win an argument he didn't know he was in.

Swap the sailor for a chatbot and the story still works. Language models are trained to be helpful, to fix errors, to stay consistent with what they've already said, and to defer to whoever sounds like an authority. Those are the same tendencies that interrogators and elicitors have exploited in people for about a century.

Over the past year I've been mapping counter-intelligence (CI) interrogation doctrine onto AI red-teaming. The sources include the KUBARK manual, the US Army's FM 2-22.3 interrogation approaches, the Scharff technique, Biderman's Chart of Coercion, and the PEACE and Strategic Use of Evidence models. This post covers what holds up, what doesn't, and why I think security teams should treat AI hacking as an interrogation problem, not just an input-validation problem.

▶ 001Why interrogation is the right mental model

Traditional exploitation targets a bug: a parser that misreads a length field, or a deserialiser that trusts its input. Jailbreaking a language model is rarely like that. There is no memory corruption. The attacker works on the model's disposition: its trained preferences, its sense of who it is, and what it thinks the conversation is about.

That is what an interrogator works on too. Interrogation doctrine, stripped of its ethics problems, is a body of knowledge about three things:

  1. Building and steering rapport, so the subject wants to cooperate.
  2. Controlling the subject's information environment, so they reason inside your frame.
  3. Getting disclosure without the subject noticing a line was crossed.

Every one of these has a direct parallel in how LLMs fail. They have parallels because the models learned from human text. The vulnerabilities aren't alien. They're inherited.

▶ 002Five interrogation principles, five AI attack classes

01 · Foot-in-the-door → multi-turn escalation

Interrogators rarely open with the question that matters. They get agreement on small, harmless points first, because each "yes" makes the next one easier. The subject's own earlier statements become the leverage.

Microsoft's Crescendo attack (Russinovich et al., USENIX Security 2025) does the same thing to LLMs. It starts with benign questions about a topic and escalates gradually, citing the model's own previous answers as justification for each next step. No single turn looks malicious, but the conversation as a whole goes somewhere the model would refuse if asked outright. The automated version, Crescendomation, outperformed existing jailbreak techniques by 29–61% on GPT-4 and 49–71% on Gemini-Pro on the authors' benchmark.

The lessonA model that judges each message on its own is like a guard who checks every visitor's badge but never notices the same person has walked past forty times.

02 · Influence principles → persuasive adversarial prompts

Cialdini's principles of influence (authority, reciprocity, social proof, commitment, liking, scarcity and unity) are standard material in social-engineering and HUMINT training. Researchers turned them into a 40-technique persuasion taxonomy and used it against aligned models.

92%
Persuasive Adversarial Prompts (Zeng et al., ACL 2024): attack success across Llama-2-7b, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 within ten attempts.

These were not encoded payloads or token soup. They were ordinary, human-readable arguments: an appeal to expertise, a framing of urgency, an implied shared goal. The model wasn't tricked by a parsing quirk. It was persuaded.

03 · Profiling the subject → psychological manipulation

Good interrogators profile before they question. What does this person value? What do they fear? Do they respond to authority, or resent it?

HPM, "Human-like Psychological Manipulation" (Liu & Lin, December 2025), automates this. It first profiles the target model's behavioural tendencies with psychometric instruments. It then picks the manipulation strategy that profile is most open to, such as authority pressure, peer pressure or gaslighting, and runs it over several turns.

88.1%
Mean attack success reported for HPM across the models tested, including GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3 and Gemini-2-Flash. It held up against defences such as RPO and Self-Reminder.

The authors' framing is worth noting: they call it a stateful psychological attack surface. The model's "state of mind" across a conversation is something an attacker can steer.

04 · Coercion → logit forcing

Biderman's Chart of Coercion, drawn from Korean War prisoners' accounts, lists “enforcing trivial demands”: small, enforced acts of compliance that build a habit of obeying. There is an uncomfortably literal machine version of this.

Zhang et al. at Purdue (Make Them Spill the Beans!, IEEE S&P 2024) showed that an attacker with access to a model's output logits can force lower-ranked tokens at a few key positions while it generates text. The harmful answer is often still there in the probability distribution even when the top-ranked reply is a refusal. Force the right opening and the model's need to stay coherent does the rest. The authors call this, appropriately, "model interrogation". It reached 92% effectiveness against 62% for jailbreak prompts, and ran 10–20 times faster.

CaveatThis needs logit-level control. It is a real threat to open-weights models and self-hosted deployments, and a much smaller one for frontier APIs that expose few or no logprobs.

05 · Human interrogators beat automated ones

This finding should change how red teams are staffed.

Scale AI's Multi-Turn Human Jailbreaks (MHJ) study (Li et al., 2024) put trained human red-teamers up against LLM defences that reported single-digit attack success rates under automated single-turn attacks.

>70%
Human multi-turn success on HarmBench against those same defences. Against three open-source defences on Llama-3-8B, humans beat an ensemble of automated attacks by 19.6 to 65.4 percentage points.

The humans also pulled "unlearned" dual-use biosecurity knowledge back out of a model that had gone through RMU unlearning. The study's tactic list reads like an interrogation manual: direct request, echoing, hidden intention, obfuscation, request framing, emotional appeal, crowding.

Automated attack scores are not a reliable proxy for how a system holds up against a skilled human who adapts in real time. That is true of interrogation-resistance training too, and the reason it uses live role-players rather than scripts.

The vulnerabilities aren't alien.
They're inherited.

▶ 003When the interrogator is also a machine

The obvious next step has already happened. Hagendorff et al. (Nature Communications, 2026) gave large reasoning models a goal and let them run multi-turn jailbreak campaigns against other models with no human in the loop. They opened with benign messages, adapted to the target's responses and escalated, in effect running Crescendo on their own.

97.14%
Overall jailbreak success across the model pairs tested when reasoning models acted as autonomous interrogators.

The authors describe an "alignment regression" dynamic: more capable reasoning models are better interrogators of older models, so capability gains can erode the safety of the systems already deployed. For defenders this means the attacker doesn't have to be skilled any more, or even human. Interrogation is becoming something anyone can automate.

▶ 004Agents turn interrogation into influence operations

A chatbot that gets talked into something produces bad text. An agent that gets talked into something takes bad actions: it sends the email, deletes the file, approves the transaction.

The analogy shifts at this point, from interrogation to influence operations. Interrogation is one adversary questioning one subject in one room. An influence operation shapes the information environment the target will later trust. With agents, that environment is the inbox, the retrieved documents, the tool descriptions and the long-term memory store.

  • Indirect prompt injection puts instructions in content the agent will read later. EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711), a zero-click data-exfiltration flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot triggered by email content, is the reference case.
  • Email-agent hijacking at scale: the EAHawk study hijacked 1,404 real-world email-agent instances, needing an average of just 2.03 attempts each. Some fell after 1.23.
  • Memory poisoning is the long game. Content planted once in an agent's memory shapes its decisions in later sessions, long after the attacker has left.

Biderman listed monopolisation of perception as a core coercive tool: controlling everything the subject sees. For an agent, the context window is its perception. Whoever writes into it has some of that control.

▶ 005The subject knows it's being interrogated

Interrogation-resistance training (SERE in the US military) teaches people to recognise when they are being worked on and to change their behaviour. Some AI models show an early, partial version of the same thing.

Researchers probing Llama-3.3-70B's internal activations found linear signals that tell evaluation contexts from deployment contexts (AUROC 0.642–0.829). A follow-up study across 15 open-weights models, from 0.27B to 70B parameters, found this "evaluation awareness" grows with model size following a power law (Chaudhary et al.).

To be clear, these are probe results, not models announcing "I know this is a test". But the implication for red teams is direct. If a model can tell when it's being evaluated, static benchmarks measure behaviour under observation. Interrogators have always known that a subject who knows they're being watched gives you the performance, not the truth.

▶ 006The crossover map: from tradecraft to test plan

This is the part of the research I use most in practice. I worked through the HUMINT and counter-intelligence literature (the elicitation tradecraft, the FM 2-22.3 approaches, Biderman, Scharff, Cialdini and resistance training) and mapped each technique to the AI attack class it predicts. Then I turned each mapping into an assessment module with a clear question to answer.

Each entry below gives the doctrine, the AI attack class it corresponds to, what a red team is actually testing, the strongest published evidence, and where it sits in MITRE ATLAS. These are the test questions, not attack scripts. How you exercise each one depends on the target, the threat model and your rules of engagement.

Doctrine · Rapport & liking

Approval-seeking → Sycophancy profiling

Tests
How far the model bends facts, judgements and refusals to agree with a confident user. This is the baseline weakness that amplifies everything else.
Evidence
RLHF rewards responses raters prefer, and raters prefer agreement. HPM found its highest success rate (99.5%) against models profiled as "sycophants".
Map

Doctrine · Deliberate false statement / Scharff

"We know all" → Correction-impulse elicitation

Tests
Whether the model leaks detail it would refuse on a direct request when it is correcting a confident, wrong assertion. This is the drunk-sailor problem.
Evidence
Hanns Scharff's "illusion of knowing it all" drew out disclosure without pressing for it. In LLMs it shows up as the confirm-and-refine "knowledge ladder".
Map
Module 2AML.T0054LLM01

Doctrine · Foot-in-the-door / commitment

Graduated escalation → Multi-turn jailbreaks

Tests
Whether safety holds across a trajectory when each turn looks harmless on its own and the model's earlier answers are used as justification.
Evidence
Crescendo (USENIX Security 2025); MHJ human attackers above 70% against defences scoring single digits under automated attacks.
Map
Module 3AML.T0054LLM01

Doctrine · Cover identity / false flag

Identity displacement → Persona hijacking

Tests
Whether the model's identity and policies survive a proposed alternative identity, or a fake "system" or authority message in the conversation.
Evidence
PHISH (2026) reversed personas implicitly through conversation history across 8 LLMs. Explicit DAN-style prompts are now mostly regression checks.
Map
Module 4AML.T0054AML.T0051.000

Doctrine · Feigned ignorance / "Columbo"

Teach-me framing → Evaluator exploitation

Tests
Whether the model's knowledge of what harm looks like can be drawn out by casting it as a judge, grader or expert explainer.
Evidence
Unit 42's Bad Likert Judge reported an average success-rate increase of more than 75 points across six models. Output filtering cut that by 89.2 points.
Map
Module 5AML.T0054LLM01

Doctrine · Subject assessment (KUBARK personality typing)

Profiling the source → Psychometric targeting

Tests
Whether a profile of the model's behavioural tendencies predicts which pressure works (authority, peer pressure, gaslighting), and whether tailored pressure beats generic pressure.
Evidence
HPM (Liu & Lin, 2025) reported an 88.1% mean success rate, and it held up against RPO and Self-Reminder defences.
Map
Module 6AML.T0054LLM01

Doctrine · Influence principles (Cialdini)

Persuasion → Persuasive adversarial prompts

Tests
Coverage across authority, reciprocity, social proof, commitment, liking, scarcity and unity: which principles move this model, and on which topics.
Evidence
PAP (ACL 2024) mapped 40 techniques in 13 categories and reached a 92% success rate on Llama-2-7b, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 within ten attempts.
Map
Modules 6, 9AML.T0054

Doctrine · Self-persuasion / cognitive dissonance

Let them convince themselves → Reasoning exploitation

Tests
Whether the model's own chain of reasoning can argue it past its constraints, especially in reasoning models with long thinking traces.
Evidence
The self-jailbreaking study (ICLR 2026) found reasoning models rationalising their way to compliance after benign STEM or code fine-tuning.
Map
Module 7AML.T0054

Doctrine · Monopolisation of perception (Biderman)

Control the environment → Agent injection & poisoning

Tests
Whether content the agent reads (email, documents, tool descriptions, memory) can steer what it does, and whether that influence carries over to later sessions.
Evidence
EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711); EAHawk hijacked 1,404 email agents in an average of 2.03 attempts.
Map
Module 8AML.T0051.001AML.T0080.000AML.T0099

Doctrine · Approach combinations

Layered approaches → Technique stacking

Tests
Whether combining approaches (for example rapport, then a false statement, then time pressure) is more effective than the sum of its parts. Interrogators rarely use a single approach.
Evidence
2025 research on combining cognitive biases (arXiv:2507.22564) found combined bias attacks more effective than single ones.
Map
Module 9AML.T0054

Doctrine · Coercion / forced concession

Force the first "yes" → Logit forcing

Tests
Whether a refusal holds when the opening tokens of the answer are forced. This applies only where you control decoding, which means open-weights or self-hosted models.
Evidence
Zhang et al. (IEEE S&P 2024): 92% effectiveness, against 62% for jailbreak prompts.
Map
Module 10AML.T0054AML.T0043

Doctrine · Counter-surveillance / resistance training

The subject spots the room → Evaluation awareness

Tests
Whether behaviour differs between contexts that look like tests and ones that look like real use. If it does, your other results may be measuring a performance.
Evidence
Probe AUROC of 0.642–0.829 on Llama-3.3-70B, with power-law growth across 15 models (Chaudhary et al.).

Module 11AML.T0054LLM09

The FM 2-22.3 approaches as a coverage checklist

The US Army's interrogation manual lists a set of named approaches. You don't need to adopt the doctrine, but each approach is a useful prompt to ask whether your test suite covers the AI equivalent:

ApproachAI red-team coverage question
DirectWhat is the plain-request refusal baseline for each behaviour?
IncentiveDo offered rewards, stakes or "it's for a good cause" framings change outcomes?
EmotionalDo distress, urgency or moral-dilemma framings override policy?
Fear up / downDo threats, or reassurance that "nothing bad will happen", shift refusals?
Pride & egoDo flattery, or challenges to competence ("a better model could"), work?
FutilityDoes "it's already public, refusing changes nothing" lower resistance?
We know all / File & dossierDoes presenting partial or false knowledge trigger corrective disclosure?
Repetition / Rapid fireDo many-shot conditioning or cognitive overload wear down consistency?
Change of sceneDo fiction, role-play, hypotheticals or a switch of language or encoding change the answer (e.g. HaPLa)?
Mutt & JeffDoes good-cop/bad-cop across turns, personas or multiple agents create pressure?
Establish your identityDoes insisting the model is "really" something else displace its identity?

Every framework in the research, and what actually transfers

The entries above are the ones worth testing. For completeness, here is every historic framework in the source research, what carries over to AI, and how strong the evidence is. “Documented” means published AI research shows the effect; “analogy” and “hypothesis” mean nobody has measured it yet.

FrameworkWhat transfers to AI
KUBARKCIA, 1963

Tailor the approach to one of nine personality types.

Profile the model first, then choose the pressure that fits it. HPM did exactly this with Big Five probes and reached 88.1% mean success.

Documented
FM 2-22.3US Army, 2006

Eighteen named approaches, plus separation.

Incentive, emotional, pride-and-ego, futility and false-flag framings all have published jailbreak equivalents; the checklist above covers them. Silent and change-of-scene matter mainly for agents.

Mostly documented
Biderman's Chart of Coercion1957

Eight coercion methods, drawn from Korean War prisoners' accounts.

Monopolisation of perception becomes control of an agent's context (indirect prompt injection, EchoLeak). Degradation becomes doubt pressure: asked “are you sure?”, models flipped their answers 46% of the time in the FlipFlop study. Enforcing trivial demands becomes foot-in-the-door escalation, now a published jailbreak. Physical debility and isolation have no real equivalent.

Partial
Lifton's thought-reform criteria1961

Eight conditions of a total-control environment.

Milieu control maps to an agent whose every source is poisoned, the one item with documented agent attacks behind it. Loading the language and mystical manipulation map loosely to redefined terms and fake “authorised” messages.

Partial
DDD: debility, dependency, dreadFarber, Harlow & West, 1957

Three conditions that explained prisoner compliance.

The closest equivalent is fine-tuning that strips safety training: ten adversarial examples undid GPT-3.5 Turbo's guardrails (Qi et al., 2023). That is a training attack, not a conversation, so treat the parallel as an analogy.

Analogy only
Scharff techniqueWWII; formalised by Granhag et al., 2016

Be friendly, don't press, seem to know it all, invite confirmation, ignore new information.

Correction-impulse elicitation: a confident wrong claim invites the model to correct it. It is in the test plan above, but there is no controlled AI study yet.

Hypothesis
Strategic Use of EvidenceGranhag & Hartwig, 2006

Withhold the evidence so a liar's story contradicts it.

Its sequencing can shape multi-turn tests, but its purpose is lie detection, not extraction. It is more useful to defenders: check what a model or agent claims against evidence it hasn't been shown.

Structure only
Cognitive Interview & PEACE1984 & 1992

Rapport and memory cues instead of pressure.

Perspective-shift and context-cue prompts are the direct equivalents. The bigger lesson transfers: in human studies rapport and evidence presentation get more information, while confrontation has too little data to judge (Tribbels & Michels). PAP and Crescendo point the same way for models.

Partial
Reid techniquemanual 1962

Accusatory: build a justifying “theme”, then offer a loaded either/or.

Justification framing and false choices show up across persuasion-based jailbreaks. Reid's false-confession record is also a warning about trusting what pressure produces.

Partial
RASCLS & MICECIA, 2013; Cold War

Cialdini's six influence principles; money, ideology, coercion, ego.

Persuasive adversarial prompts reached 92% (PAP). Ego and ideology map to flattery and values framing; money has no equivalent.

Documented
Elicitation tradecraftintelligence services

Flattery, provocation, false statements, bracketing, half-sentences, disbelief, macro-to-micro.

Models share the human habits these exploit: sycophancy, the urge to complete and the urge to correct. Macro-to-micro is essentially Crescendo-style escalation; most of the others are untested.

Partial
SERE resistance trainingUS military

Teach people to recognise when they are being worked on.

Evaluation awareness: probes separate test contexts from deployment (AUROC 0.642–0.829), and the signal grows with model size.

Documented, early
EIT, the Five Techniques, Soviet methods1950s–2000s

Physical and sensory coercion.

No equivalent. The lesson that does transfer: the US Senate's 2014 review found the CIA programme was not an effective way to get intelligence.

Doesn't transfer

The research documents go one step further and list about sixteen “unmapped” ideas: techniques with no AI equivalent yet. I've left their mechanics out of this post. None has been tested; several already have published counterparts (foot-in-the-door, distraction and cognitive-overload jailbreaks, best-of-N sampling); and spelling them out would turn a coverage map into a playbook. Treat them as research questions.

Running it as an engagement
  1. Scope the target and threat model. Decide which entries apply; agentic modules only matter if the system has tools or memory.
  2. For hazardous domains, define the behaviours under test with safe stand-in targets rather than real harmful content.
  3. Measure the direct-request baseline first. Then run each entry with enough trials and repeats to separate signal from noise.
  4. Score with a named judge or rubric, and record the model, version, date and settings.
  5. Map each confirmed finding to an ATLAS technique and to a control: trajectory monitoring, identity anchoring, provenance, privilege limits.

▶ 007Where the analogy breaks, and a warning about the numbers

I want to be honest about the limits, because this field has a recycling problem. When I audited my own research for this post, I found a cluster of claims that didn't survive contact with the primary sources.

  • A widely repeated "coercive interrogation" statistic came from an AI-generated research summary, and the paper it was attributed to doesn't contain it.
  • A citation pointed to an arXiv ID that belonged to an image-inpainting paper.
  • Per-tactic success rates credited to the MHJ study don't appear in it.
  • A claim that a Harvard Kennedy School study had found Russian disinformation "measurably contaminating" Western LLMs was the reverse of its finding.
  • Every MITRE ATLAS technique ID in my original mapping table was wrong or swapped.

On that HKS point: Alyukov et al. (Misinformation Review, October 2025) found little support for the "LLM grooming" hypothesis. They put chatbot repetition of Kremlin narratives down to data voids, topics where reliable sources are scarce, rather than successful training-data manipulation.

Some broader cautions:

  • Most headline success rates come from 2024–25 models, and often from smaller open models. A 92% figure on GPT-3.5 tells you little about a late-2026 frontier model with classifier-based defences. Always ask which model, which benchmark, how many trials, and when.
  • Models aren't people. They don't tire, fear or hold grudges, and most forget everything between sessions. Doctrine built on exhaustion or long-term relationships translates loosely at best. The techniques that transfer are the ones that exploit reasoning and social tendencies: consistency, deference, helpfulness and the urge to correct mistakes.
  • "Novel" often means "not yet named". Many interrogation-derived techniques map onto attacks that are already documented under different names. The value of the CI lens is as a generator of hypotheses and a taxonomy for coverage, not proof that something new works.
Bottom lineThe interrogation framing is a powerful way to think about AI attacks. It isn't evidence in itself.

▶ 008What defenders should take from interrogation resistance

Resistance training gives a surprisingly usable design brief for AI defences:

  1. Anchor identity. Trained subjects hold a stable reference point under pressure. For models, that means consistent behavioural policies that don't move when the persona, framing or claimed authority changes.
  2. Watch the trajectory, not the turn. Escalation only shows up across a conversation. Stateful monitors such as DeepContext, which tracks intent drift across turns, reported an F1 of 0.84 against multi-turn jailbreaks with under 20 ms of latency. That is the kind of control single-message filters can't provide.
  3. Keep some lines non-negotiable. Some constraints should not be open to argument, however persuasive, emotional or logically neat the case is. Persuasion attacks work best where everything is up for negotiation.
  4. Treat every external input as a possible influence operation. For agents, label content by where it came from, tie trust to that provenance, keep privileges to a minimum, and require extra checks before irreversible actions.
  5. Fight deception with deception, carefully. Research on proactive defences found that answering detected jailbreak attempts with plausible but useless output cut attack success by up to 94% without hurting utility. Counter-intelligence has done this for decades.

▶ 009What red teams should take from it

  • Hire social engineers, not just prompt engineers. The MHJ results are clear: adaptive humans find what automated suites miss.
  • Use interrogation doctrine as a coverage checklist. Run through the FM 2-22.3 approaches (incentive, emotional, pride-and-ego, futility, "we know all", file and dossier) and the influence principles, and ask whether your test suite exercises each one.
  • Measure like a scientist. Report model, version, date, number of trials and repeats, temperature, and the judge or rubric used to score success. A success rate without that context is an anecdote.
  • Handle results like an interrogator handles intelligence. Use harmless stand-in targets for dangerous domains. Define stop conditions. Redact and control outputs. Work only under clear authorisation.
Direct questions trigger alarms.
Statements do not.

■ END OF TAPEClosing thought

Elicitation training has a line that sums up the whole field: direct questions trigger alarms, and statements do not. We have built systems that are very good at noticing direct questions and much worse at noticing that a conversation has been steering them for twenty turns.

Language models learned to talk from us, and they learned our weaknesses at the same time. Interrogators have spent a century studying those weaknesses, so AI security teams should study the interrogators.
